title: Entering the room
hook: Balaam's words "how goodly are thy tents" are said on entering a synagogue

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev, the service of the heart. Your line was prayer is the heart's work. Which sentence did you mean completely? Today, the siddur's first words for many people, said at the door. Day five hundred forty-one.

Doorways change people. You lower your voice walking into a library. You straighten your back at the door of a job interview. At some homes you take your shoes off before you're even asked. Something in us knows a threshold is a small border. In many synagogues, the first words people say on entering come from a surprising source. They were first spoken by a foreign prophet who had been hired to curse.
screen: `QUIET IN THE LIBRARY.` → `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `WORDS FROM A HIRED PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Back in Numbers, King Balak of Moab hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam climbs a height, looks down at the camp spread across the valley, tribe by tribe, and blessing comes out of his mouth instead: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, mah tovu: how good. What did he see down there? The Talmud, in Bava Batra, and Rashi after it, point to a detail. The tents were set up so that no doorway faced another doorway. Each family had its privacy. A huge camp, and no one peering into anyone else's home. The respect was visible from the hilltop. Tradition read tents and dwellings as more than tents. The rabbis took them as houses of prayer and houses of study. So the verse became words for entering a synagogue. In many siddurim, mah tovu stands at the very beginning of the morning prayers, followed by a psalm verse about coming into God's house through God's great kindness. There's a twist worth noticing. These are the words of an outsider, someone sent to do harm, who looked closely and saw goodness. A few later teachers were uneasy about opening prayer with Balaam's words. The custom stayed. Some readers find it moving that, in many prayer books, the morning begins with what a stranger saw: a community that respects one another's doors.
screen: `BALAAM, HIRED TO CURSE.` · `MAH TOVU: HOW GOOD.` · `NO DOOR FACING ANOTHER.` · `AN OUTSIDER'S WORDS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `HOW GOOD THESE TENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause at one doorway. Settle, and breathe. Picture the next doorway you'll walk through: a home, a classroom, an office, a place of worship. See yourself stopping just before it, for a single breath. If you pray, mah tovu is there: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob. If not, simply notice what's good about the place you're about to enter, and about the people inside it. Then picture stepping through. The bell holds the time.
Entering the room. Mah tovu, how good: Balaam's blessing, said at the synagogue door.
Your line: how good these tents. Today, before you walk into one room, pause and find one good thing about it, or its people. Day five hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Many Jews say mah tovu (Numbers 24:5) on entering a synagogue in the morning, followed by verses from the Psalms; in many siddurim it is the first passage of the morning service.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about tents.
what it means: an outsider sent to curse sees a community that respects one another's privacy, and blesses it.
what a scholar hears: Bava Batra 60a and Rashi: no doorway faced another; Sanhedrin 105b reads the tents as houses of prayer and study.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 60a; Rashi on Numbers 24:2, 24:5

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'Many find it moving that the prayer book begins' softened to 'some readers... in many prayer books', since placement varies by rite.
Numbers 24:5 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Bava Batra 60a: Balaam saw that the openings of their tents did not face each other; Rashi on Numbers 24:2/24:5. Sanhedrin 105b: tents and dwellings as synagogues and study houses. Paraphrased.
Objection to opening with Balaam's words is associated with the Maharshal (16th century); kept as 'a few later teachers'.
Placement of mah tovu at the start of the morning service varies by rite (common in Ashkenazi siddurim).
Balaam was covered in Block C (Balak); the review of this day refers back to it lightly.
